sources.title: Chocolate Crumble and Snapping / Cutting ( Moderately thick and hard dark chocolate ).wav
sources.author: Finnssound

choco-snap.notes: Real chocolate being broken. 01-02 are the two clean, isolated block snaps (3.0 s and 4.6 s) of pbeare70's 'posh chocolate' recording (the rest of that file is wrapper rustle); 03-06 are crack events from Finnssound's recording of hard dark baking chocolate about 1 cm thick (8.49, 2.55, 10.56 and 11.23 s; the rest of that file is plastic wrapper twisting and table thumps). CC0 offers only about six clean single snaps in total, so the minimum count of 6 is used; 03-06 carry the crack plus one or two small crumble clicks after it. A 150 Hz high-pass removes the table thump, a 9 kHz low-pass takes the edge off, and every slice starts on its first spike. Check first: RMS spreads -27 to -20 dBFS, spread 7.3 dB because the snaps differ in body; 03 (hf>6 kHz 39%) and 02 (18%) are the brightest, so listen for harshness there. A CC BY search found only a single 0.4 s snap (#586993) and a very quiet breaking recording (#764746), neither used.
choco-snap.process: Source #851574 (Freesound preview -hq.mp3 decoded to 16-bit WAV with ffmpeg at native 44100 Hz, channels averaged to mono). Filters on the whole recording before cutting: 2nd-order Butterworth 150 Hz high-pass and 9 kHz low-pass (scipy.signal.sosfilt, causal). Slice onset = first 1 ms block above 12% of the event's own peak, slice starts 3.5 ms before it; 2 ms linear fade-in, 40 ms raised-cosine fade-out, then each slice peak-normalised to 0.85 (gain below). Slices as file: file start in source s / transient onset in source s / length ms / gain dB: 01: 2.992 / 2.996 / 108 / +1.2; 02: 4.575 / 4.579 / 110 / -1.3. Source #660866 (Freesound preview -hq.mp3 decoded to 16-bit WAV with ffmpeg at native 48000 Hz, channels averaged to mono). Filters on the whole recording before cutting: 2nd-order Butterworth 150 Hz high-pass and 9 kHz low-pass (scipy.signal.sosfilt, causal). Slice onset = first 1 ms block above X% of the event's own peak (X per slice: 03: 30%, 04: 12%, 05: 30%, 06: 30%), slice starts 3.5 ms before it; 2 ms linear fade-in, 40 ms raised-cosine fade-out, then each slice peak-normalised to 0.85 (gain below). jelly-squish.notes: Real jelly (Jello, tagged strawberry) being mangled on a plate, from a pack the author recorded for a game. Each slice is one wet burst, a squish transient plus a short resonant tail, 126-200 ms, chosen as single-burst events of similar level (RMS -25 to -23 dBFS, spread 2.4 dB). A 5.5 kHz low-pass tames the wet clicks (the raw recording has its centroid at 4-6 kHz). It is a wet squelch with no pitched bloop, so it stays distinct from rainbow/jelly-land (bubble bloops). Check first: 03 and 04 are the brightest (centroid about 4.3 kHz, hf>6 kHz 11-17%). Source noise floor -60 dBFS; a faint 1.54 kHz line appears in the gaps (probably plate or jelly resonance), more than 35 dB under the events.

Slice onset = first 1 ms block above 5% of the event's own peak, slice starts 3 ms before it; 2 ms linear fade-in, 50 ms raised-cosine fade-out, then each slice peak-normalised to 0.85 (gain below). sources.title: Hit on stuffed animals - ZOOM H2N.flac
sources.author: RanneM

mallow-press.notes: No CC0 recording of an actual marshmallow turned up, so this uses the closest soft, dull 'fwump' found: hits on stuffed animals (plush toys) recorded with a Zoom H2n. Each slice is one soft thump of 123-165 ms whose energy sits mostly at 200-800 Hz, with essentially nothing above 3 kHz (120 Hz high-pass, 3.2 kHz low-pass); RMS -21 to -17 dBFS, spread 4.2 dB. Check first: 01 is the lowest (centroid about 390 Hz) and may be weak on laptop speakers, and the texture may read as pillow rather than marshmallow. Source noise floor -66 dBFS with a faint 54 Hz hum line (below the high-pass); the recording contains one clipped sample, not inside any slice. Two bass-heavy events from the same recording were dropped.

choco-plop.notes: Hands slathered with syrup and slapped/slopped around: each slice is one viscous slap, a sharp wet onset followed by a smooth 100-250 ms decay, which is what a heavy landing in thick melted chocolate should do. Very uniform set (244-331 ms, centroid 1198-2330 Hz, RMS -23 to -20 dBFS, spread 3.1 dB). 5 kHz low-pass and 80 Hz high-pass. The source is hot (peak -0.5 dBFS) but not clipped; its noise floor is -52 dBFS with a faint 117 Hz hum line, both about 50 dB under the events. A brighter eighth slice (centroid 3.3 kHz) was dropped as an outlier.

choco-bubble-loop.notes: Home-made tomato sauce simmering on low heat: thick, round bubbles at roughly 8-10 per second, soft 'blup' pops with 86% of the energy between 200 and 2000 Hz and almost nothing above 4 kHz; the 103 s source looks steady throughout in the overview spectrogram. A thick-sauce stand-in for melted chocolate bubbling. Mono (source L/R correlation 0.96), 3.200 s, seamless (tiled three times: no step or level jump at the seams). Check first: it is a tomato-sauce recording, so the bubbles may read as boiling rather than chocolate. Rejected: #560564 (brighter, with stirring), #627662 (very quiet, high-frequency crackle), #249528 and #444473 (bass-heavy porridge), #315915 and #638628 (almost everything below 400 Hz).
choco-bubble-loop.process: Source #124584 (Freesound preview -hq.mp3 decoded to 16-bit stereo WAV with ffmpeg at 44100 Hz), channels averaged to mono. Loop body = source 3.500 s to 6.700 s (3.200 s). The next 150 ms of the source (6.700-6.850 s) are crossfaded into the first 150 ms of the body with an equal-power cos/sin curve, so the end of the file flows into its beginning. DC removed, 80 Hz high-pass and 12 kHz low-pass (2nd-order Butterworth), peak-normalised to 0.7 (gain +7.0 dB).
